title: Short Stuff: All about BPAs
summary: Short Stuff episode on bisphenol A (BPA), hosted with Josh and Chuck sitting in for a day (Speaker 3 is also a host voice). Covers what BPA is and where it appears (plastics, polycarbonate, can linings, dental work, contact lens cases, baby bottles, thermal paper receipts), the late-1990s discovery by geneticist Patricia Hunt studying mouse ovaries, BPA as an endocrine disruptor mimicking estrogen, health concerns (diabetes, insulin resistance, PCOS, obesity, hypertension, reproductive effects, breast cancer), the US FDA's 2014 position on its safe level, the European Food Safety Authority's 2023 much lower tolerable daily intake, and substitutes like BPF and BPS and alternatives such as glass and stainless steel with plastic liners.

segments.title: Introduction and where BPA shows up
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short episode on BPA and how to pronounce it. They list common sources, including plastics, can linings, dental work, contact lens cases and baby bottles, and note thermal paper receipts as the largest average exposure.

segments.title: Patricia Hunt's discovery
segments.summary: Geneticist Patricia Hunt, studying mouse ovaries in 1998, found rising chromosomal errors and reproductive effects. She traced them to BPA in cages and water bottles, and swapping those out returned the mice to normal.

segments.title: BPA as an endocrine disruptor
segments.summary: BPA is described as an endocrine disruptor that mimics hormones, mainly affecting estrogen, which influences many genes and organs. Early regulatory reactions called the evidence inconclusive. The hosts note that low doses appeared to have worse effects than larger doses, which Josh jokingly explains with a Three Stooges analogy.

segments.title: FDA 2014 safety level
segments.summary: The FDA upheld its no observed adverse effects level after a four-year review begun in 2010, with a 2014 conclusion of five milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day. The hosts question whether typical exposure is that low.

segments.title: Health effects and the scientific debate
segments.summary: The hosts list health concerns linked to BPA, including type two diabetes, insulin resistance, polycystic ovary syndrome, obesity, high blood pressure, preterm births, developmental issues, breast cancer and tumors. They discuss the limits of proof in science and industry pushback.

segments.title: European Food Safety Authority's 2023 lower limit
segments.summary: In 2023 the European Food Safety Authority lowered its tolerable daily intake sharply, from four micrograms to 0.2 nanograms per kilogram of body weight per day. Josh says this is far below the US level and describes the agency defending its decision. He notes that one critical paper was funded by the American Chemistry Council.

segments.title: BPA-free labels and bisphenol substitutes
segments.summary: The FDA website is quoted as saying BPA is safe at current food exposure levels. The hosts advise looking for BPA-free labels, but note substitutes such as bisphenol F and bisphenol S are less studied and may be just as harmful.

segments.title: Alternatives to plastic containers
segments.summary: Glass is suggested as an alternative. Stainless steel containers often have plastic tops or liners, which may still release plastic into drinks. The hosts discuss whether plastic can be avoided entirely.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with a joke about the door and a note that Short Stuff is out, with iHeartRadio promotion.
